At this point, we leave open the kind of knowledge the policy has about the noise function ρ; one can think of different settings, where either ρ is given, ρ(xt ) is observed at time t, or is estimated from the observations. In what follows, we also rely on a frequentist notion of information gain. We assume that we are given a sequence (It )t≥1 of non-negative, continuous functions It : (X × R)t−1 × X → R≥0 , and we think of It (x) = It (x1 , y1 , . . . , xt−1 , yt−1 , x) as the information gain of evaluating x ∈ X at time t. A specific example, that we explore in greater detail later, is It (x) = log(1 + σt (x)2 /ρ(x)2 ), which in the Bayesian setting with posterior variance σt (x)2 corresponds to the mutual information I(x; f |Ft−1 ). In this case our definition of γT relates to the notion from Srinivas et al. (2010). Example 1 (Choice between low and high noise) We construct a simple bandit instance, where pairs of actions are known to yield the same value, but one action of each pair is subject to larger noise variance. By exploiting the correlation, a natural strategy is to only choose the actions with less noise to determine the pair with the largest payoff. Formally, let S be a compact set, and define X = S × {ρ1 , ρ2 } for 0 < ρ1 < ρ2 . We denote (s, ρ0 ) ∈ X for s ∈ S and ρ0 ∈ {ρ1 , ρ2 }. Further, let f belong to a parametrized family fθ∗ : X → R, such that fθ∗ (s, ρ1 ) = fθ∗ (s, ρ2 ) for all s ∈ S. We use the last coordinate to specify the noise bound ρ(s, ρ0 ) = ρ0 . Naively, any regret guarantee using a uniform noise bound degenerates as ρ2 → ∞. This seems unnecessary, as choosing (s, ρ1 ) over (s, ρ2 ) clearly yields a more efficient solution. We show that this is not the default choice for standard algorithms. Consider the widely used UCB strategy. Here, a confidence set Ct is constructed (possibly depending on ρ), containing the true parameter θ∗ with high probability. UCB then evaluates xUCB t ∈ arg maxx∈X maxθ∈Ct fθ (x). Note that the acquisition function is independent of ρ(xUCB t ), therefore UCB has no preference of ρ1 over ρ2 . The same is true for Thompson Sampling, where xTS t ∈ arg maxx∈X fθ̃ (x) is determined using a sample θ̃ from the posterior distribution of θ.
